How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX, a Haitian citizen, is appealing against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection on the grounds that he is not credible, that he failed to establish the state's inability to provide adequate protection and that the risk he might face if he were to return to Haiti is not caused by the inability of that country to provide adequate health care.
The appellant argues that the findings of fact and law are incorrect and were made improperly without regard to the evidence.

I am of the opinion that the issue of state protection, although not determinative, was analyzed incorrectly. As well, having reviewed the evidence, I find that the appellant failed to prove his allegations that his life is in danger for the reasons alleged.
The appeal is dismissed.

Before he left Haiti in XXXX 2016, the appellant was working as a XXXX for XXXX. Part of his work involved an XXXX XXXX of the XXXX XXXX XXXX branch. In a report submitted on XXXX XXXX, 2016, he identified employee XXXX XXXX as the individual responsible for a US $5 0000 fraud. Mr. XXXX, who was fired on XXXX XXXX, 2016, threatened to kill the appellant.

The facts alleged in the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) may be summarized as follows: * In the days following Mr. XXXX termination, the appellant received numerous death threats by telephone. He told his superiors about his problems, but they told him that they could not help him. * Local merchants told him that, between XXXX XXXX and XXXX, 2016, bikers had asked about his daily routine and his address. * On XXXX XXXX, 2016, he resigned from his job, changed his telephone number and stopped sleeping at home. * On XXXX XXXX, 2016, some men obtained his telephone number through a friend. The death threats then resumed. * On XXXX XXXX, 2016, he spoke with a person in charge of the National Human Rights Defense Network, who recommended that he leave the country. Three days later, she took him to the airport.

The issues to be decided by the RAD are as follows: * Did the RPD err in assessing the appellant's credibility? * Did the RPD fail to consider evidence? * Did the RPD err in finding that the appellant had failed to establish the Haitian state's inability to provide him with adequate protection? * Did the RPD err in finding that the appellant had failed to establish that the risk to his health is not caused by the inability of his country to provide health care?

Except in cases where the credibility of the oral evidence is at issue and the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage, the RAD must determine whether the RPD decision is correct.1 If there is an error of fact, of law or of mixed fact and law, the RAD must intervene through one of the means set out in sections 110 and 111 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

Should I owe deference to the RPD because it enjoys a meaningful advantage, I will indicate it in my analysis. However, deference to the RPD does not equate to a blind endorsement of its findings.2 MERITS OF THE APPEAL

The facts as alleged do not suggest a nexus between the appellant's fear and one of the five Convention grounds. The analysis will determine whether the RPD erred in finding that the appellant failed to meet the burden of proof required under paragraph 97(1)(b) and subparagraph 97(1)(b)(iv) of the IRPA. State protection
First, although it is not determinative in this case, I would like to make a few comments regarding the RPD's findings on this issue.

Because the appellant had not filed a complaint regarding the threats he claimed to have received, the RPD found that the appellant had failed to provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to provide adequate protection.
The appellant maintains that the RPD's findings are incorrect because it failed to consider the culture of vengeance in Haiti, against which the police has been largely ineffective.

With respect, like my RAD colleagues,3 I am of the opinion that the documentary evidence is unequivocal. Currently, the Haitian state is unable to protect its citizens adequately, even though some documents in the National Documentation Package (NDP) of July 31, 2017, indicate that the situation has improved somewhat.4

In X (Re) 2018 CanLII 117211 (CA IRB), my colleague Patricia O'Connor analyzed this issue in depth. Although the facts are different in each case, the RPD's findings in both cases are based primarily on the refugee protection claimants' failure to inform the authorities about their problems. Regarding state protection in Haiti, my colleague writes: [30] I begin my analysis by noting that a claimant's failure to approach the state for protection was considered by the Supreme Court in Ward. The following excerpt is instructive: "[O]nly in situations in which state protection "might reasonably have been forthcoming", will the claimant's failure to approach the state for protection defeat his claim. Put another way, the claimant will not meet the definition of "Convention refugee" where it is objectively unreasonable for the claimant not to have sought the protection of his home authorities; otherwise, the claimant need not literally approach the state."5 [32] The Appellants' testimony is corroborated by objective evidence which reveals that Haiti's efforts to provide adequate state protection remains largely ineffective. [33] A Response to Information Request (RIR) reveals that the general security situation in Haiti is unpredictable, hazardous, unstable and volatile.6 According to Human Rights Watch, the "weak capacity of the Haitian National Police (HNP) contributes to the overall insecurity in the country.7 [34] The following information from the US Bureau of Diplomatic Security is revealing: "Haitians still lack basic policing services, so many residents do not report assaults, rape, and other crimes because of lingering and too often justified perceptions of police apathy, incompetence and corruption. The Bureau adds that the PNH has a very limited response capability [...and] minimal deterrent effect on criminals". It explains that, for those reasons, more Port-au-Prince residents are turning to security systems or guards, and buying firearms for personal protection."8 [35] Moreover, according to the US Bureau of Diplomatic Security, a weak judiciary "exacerbates Haiti's security problems. Freedom House also flags the weaknesses of the judicial system, describing it as "underfunded, inefficient, and corrupt, and [...] burdened by a large backlog of cases, outdated legal codes and poor facilities."9 [37] Sources consulted in a recent RIR consider there is no state protection for targets of acts of revenge in Haiti. Other sources maintain that there is some protection but that it is inadequate. The Haitian Police lacks resources to provide protection to those targeted by revenge. A Project Leader states that police officers are also targeted by acts of revenge and are afraid of the gangs. They typically encourage the person to hide or to leave the country. A Chancellor notes that the Haitian police is a weak and underpaid institution which is easily corrupted and that many police officers were involved in abductions and crimes.10 [38] Another RIR examined the effectiveness of police protection, particularly in Port-au-Prince.11 The RIR notes that the Haitian National Police have made significant achievements in the post-earthquake period but are not yet able to protect most of their citizens. [39] Haiti is ranked as one of the most corrupt police forces in the world. Aside from numerous human rights violations, they have resisted responding to gang-related violence.12 As noted above, the new evidence submitted on appeal describes that Hurricane Matthew in 2016 further complicated efforts to stabilize the country.13 [40] One report submitted to the UN Committee on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, states that the government of Haiti recognizes that impunity exists for all crimes, including gender-based violence, and identifies the following reasons: corruption and/or politicization of the judicial system, incompetence of judges or their misunderstanding of the laws, and the insufficiency of the legal framework. Although recognizing these problems is a positive step, the Government does not propose any measures to combat them.14 One source notes that an acute lack of resources and capacity in the Haitian justice system makes it difficult for the state to prosecute and punish perpetrators, and deters victims from seeking redress.15 [41] The situation in Haiti remains problematic with one source noting that "access to justice is inadequate". Freedom House notes that the judicial system is under-resourced and inefficient and is burdened by a large backlog of cases, underpaid staff, outdated legal codes and poor facilities. Bribery is common at all levels of the judicial system.16 [42] The United States Department of State Country Report on Human Rights Practices for 2017 reports that the judiciary is subject to corruption and outside influence, there is widespread corruption, credible reports persisted of officials engaging in corrupt practices and civil society groups alleged there was widespread impunity.17 [43] Another RIR notes that despite some improvement, the general security situation in Haiti remains bad, worrisome, precarious and unpredictable.18 It is also noted that the police force does not have sufficient capacity to carry out its missions, lacks resources and "doubts have been repeatedly raised as to whether the National police force is able to guarantee the security needed to protect citizens, enforce the law and promote political stability."19

Assuming that the facts have been established, in the context of Haiti, I am not persuaded that the appellant would have obtained adequate protection even if he had filed a complaint. In my opinion, the RPD erred by applying the case law without sufficiently analyzing the context.

Moreover, although my colleague O'Connor's analysis takes into account a more recent version of the NDP, I believe that I may rely on that analysis, because I must consider the current situation in the country and because the information in the version of the NDP used in this case is essentially no different from that reported in the version my colleague considered. Credibility

The RPD stated that the appellant provided vague, evasive testimony. The RPD also pointed out the following: * The appellant failed to state in the BOC Form that, on XXXX XXXX, 2016, he attended the meeting between the XXXX XXXX and Mr. XXXX, the employee responsible for the fraud; * The control report (Exhibit C-12) contained various sections. The RPD noted that comments regarding the alleged fraud were found at the end of the report, as if they had been added to the report. The RPD stated that the appellant, when asked about this, became uncomfortable, was slow to answer the questions and adjusted his answers to account for inconsistencies; * The RPD found that the appellant, who was slow to quit his job and change his place of residence, did not demonstrate the conduct of someone who was in fear of being killed by hired assassins; * The RPD also found that his statement that the alleged hired assassins could not find him was not credible, given that his work was a 10-minute walk from his home; * The appellant did not produce evidence of his meeting with a representative of a human rights organization; and * Regarding his medical condition, the RPD found that the appellant had failed to meet his burden of proving that the risk to his life was not caused by the inability of the country to provide adequate health or medical care.

The appellant maintains that he answered to the best of his knowledge and that, with the challenge of interpretation during the hearing, he may have appeared reticent and hesitant.20 Failure to state in the BOC Form that he attended the meeting with XXXX XXXX

The RPD found that the appellant's credibility was undermined by his failure to state in the BOC Form that he attended the meeting between the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and the XXXX XXXX, who was responsible for the alleged fraud.
The appellant had no comment on this finding by the RPD.

I cannot say that the RPD erred in noting that this omission undermined the credibility of his claims regarding this issue. In my opinion, this is not an insignificant fact, since his attendance enabled the terminated employee to identify the person behind his termination.

As well, I note that the report is dated XXXX XXXX, 2016, for an audit carried out between XXXX XXXX, 2016, and XXXX XXXX, 2016. The appellant testified that he submitted the report on XXXX XXXX, 2016. However, in the BOC Form at lines 18 and 19, he writes the following:21 [Translation] . . . After I submitted my report a week later, on XXXX XXXX, 2016, he was summoned by the XXXX XXXX after the meeting Mr. XXXX was fired.

This appears contrary to the statements made at the hearing that the report was submitted on XXXX XXXX, 2016. As well, if it had been submitted a week before the meeting, why would it have been dated XXXX XXXX, 2016?

These elements, taken as a whole, lead me to conclude that the RPD did nor err in finding that the omission from the BOC Form undermined the appellant's credibility. I emphasize that this factor was not considered in isolation. Contents of the report (C-12)

The appellant stated that a XXXX client complained that transactions had been made on his account while he was living abroad. In light of this, the appellant was instructed to carry out an internal audit of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He allegedly began the audit on XXXX XXXX, 2016, and submitted a report on XXXX XXXX, 2016 (C-12).22

The RPD noted that the C-12 report contains various sections. It noted that comments on the alleged fraud were found at the end of the report, [translation] "as if they had been added to the report". The RPD also noted that the appellant, when asked about this, became uncomfortable, was slow to answer the questions and adjusted his answers to account for inconsistencies.

It is difficult for me to comment on the appellant's manner of testifying, since I did not see him testify. Moreover, I understand that the presence of an interpreter may affect a decision-maker's perception of the spontaneity of a person's testimony; however, while listening to the recording of the hearing, I did not note that interpretation-related adjustments caused the appellant's statements to be translated improperly.
While I do not doubt that the appellant worked for XXXX as a XXXX, the report filed as Exhibit C-12 seems problematic. To begin with, I only have an unsigned copy of the report.
In addition, the information on page 17 of the report, the page that the RPD believes was added to the report, states that the suspicious transactions were made on XXXX XXXX, XXXX and XXXX, 2016.
I find it surprising that it is not stated at the beginning of the report that an alleged fraud is the reason for the special audit.

The following appears at the beginning of the report: [translation] "For this period, we used audit sampling to examine items posted by the XXXX on the following days: XXXX XXXX, 2016, XXXX XXXX, 2016, XXXX XXXX, 2016, and XXXX XXXX, 2016."23 I am surprised that the audit samples did not include the days on which the alleged frauds were committed.

The appellant stated that he began his audit on XXXX XXXX, 2016, and submitted his report on XXXX XXXX, 2016. In light of that, I find it odd to read the following on page 11 of the report: [translation] "During the week of XXXX XXXX to XXXX, we audited each XXXX XXXX."24

These examples of inconsistencies in the report, taken as a whole, lead me to find that the RPD did not err in harbouring some doubt based on the fact that the comments regarding the fraud seem to have been added to the initial report. Delay in leaving his employment

The appellant claims that his life has been in danger since Mr. XXXX was fired on XXXX XXXX, 2016. Mr. XXXX allegedly threatened him directly and hired assassins to murder him. The assassins allegedly looked for him in his neighbourhood on or about XXXX XXXX, 2016, and a certain XXXX, working for Mr. XXXX, telephoned him to threaten him with retaliation.
The RPD stated that the fact that the appellant continued to work at the XXXX until XXXX XXXX, 2016, suggests that he was not subjected to the alleged danger to his life.
The appellant did not file any submissions specifically to challenge this finding.

It is not wrong to consider a refugee protection claimant's conduct in response to the alleged danger.25. Moreover, in this case, the evidence shows that, three months before he left the country, the appellant had planned to travel to the United States and then to Canada.26 When asked why he had not left his employment earlier, the appellant stated that his annual leave was scheduled for XXXX XXXX, 2016.

This explanation is surprising. According to his statements, Mr. XXXX had hired assassins. They had been looking for him since XXXX XXXX, 2016, to kill him. In addition, there were numerous threats by telephone. The fact that the appellant continued to work until the day before his vacation raises serious doubt and suggests that the risk was not as alleged. Ability of hired assassins to locate the appellant
The RPD found it not to be credible that the hired assassins were unable to locate the appellant when he was working close to his home.

This finding must be considered in the Haitian context. On one hand, it was stated that the appellant cannot live safely elsewhere in the country because the hired assassins who are looking for him are powerful and part of a network. On the other hand, he was working 10 minutes from home, and the hired assassins could not find him when he left work. In my opinion, this adds to the serious doubt maintained by the decision-maker as to the appellant's claim that he is being pursued by hired assassins.27 Corroborating evidence

The RPD determined that the lack of corroborating evidence of the meeting between the appellant and a person in charge of a human rights organization undermined the credibility of his claims in that regard.

Corroborating physical evidence is not required. However, in this case, since it is a friend of the appellant, it is odd that he did not try to obtain such evidence. Appellant's health problems and exception under subparagraph 97(1)(b)(iv) of the IRPA

During the hearing, the appellant filed a letter from the McGill University Health Centre stating that he had a serious kidney disease and an article from the Internet stating that there was a shortage of equipment in the dialysis unit of the Hôpital de l'Université d'État d'Haïti (HUEH). The appellant stated that he did not know whether such treatment was available in Haiti.
The RPD found that the appellant had failed to establish that the risk he would face if he were to return "is not caused by the inability of that country to provide adequate health or medical care."

The appellant maintains that it is a combination of factors that prevents him from returning to Haiti. First are the problems associated with the fact that he identified Mr. XXXX as being responsible for a fraud at a XXXX XXXX and the problems related to his health. As well, it is stated, [translation] "It is clear that the appellant's state of health requires frequent care, specifically three times per week, and that he will not be able to obtain this in Haiti . . . these health care services are available only in a hospital [...] however, given the threats, . . . he would not be able to escape from his attackers to another area without putting his life at risk owing to the unavailability of dialysis treatments in another area."28
He states that his life is at risk by reason of the threats in combination with the health care and [translation] "not because of his country's inability to provide appropriate health care."29

With respect and due regard to the appellant's medical condition, I do not find that the RPD erred. In my opinion, the submissions filed on appeal are a mixture of submissions regarding internal flight alternatives (IFAs) and the risk of return resulting from the appellant's illness and the difficulty, if not impossibility, of obtaining adequate health care services for his illness.

During the hearing, the appellant was asked about the possibility of relocating, namely to Port-de-Paix or Cap-Haitien. However, it was argued that he would not be safe because Mr. XXXX and his associates were part of a network. It was also submitted that it would be unreasonable for him to relocate because of his condition.
However, in this case, the issue of an IFA was not addressed in the RPD's decision.

During the hearing before the RPD, it was also argued that it is difficult to get a kidney transplant in Haiti, that the appellant's medical condition requires hemodialysis three times per week, and that, according to Exhibit C-17, part of the equipment for that kind of treatment was not functioning properly.

Consequently, I am not satisfied that the RPD erred in assessing the appellant's risk of return under subparagraph 97(1)(b)(iv) of the IRPA. I note that the RPD determined that the appellant had failed to prove the facts as alleged, in particular that his life was at risk because of the alleged termination of Mr. XXXX.

Apart from problems with respect to insecurity, malfunction and access to treatments, the appellant failed to provide other reasons why he could not obtain access to these treatments. The RPD therefore did not err in finding that the appellant failed to establish that the risk by reason of his medical condition was "not caused by the inability of that country to provide adequate health or medical care."
For these reasons, I am of the opinion that the RPD rendered the correct decision despite its incorrect analysis of state protection, which was not determinative in this case.
For these reasons, I confirm the RPD's determination that XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" under section 97 of the IRPA.
